title: Memory techniques for high-volume facts
introHtml: Every field has a large amount of material that has no logic of its own: vocabulary and grammar exceptions, dates, article numbers in a legal code, formulas and constants, anatomy, drug side effects, chord shapes. Understanding helps you organise it, but in the end you simply have to hold it. For that material, spaced flashcards plus a few memory tricks work best.

items.title: Anki and flashcards done well
items.leadHtml: Make cards within 24 hours of the lecture or chapter. Do reviews every day before adding new cards. Keep one idea per card. Use cloze deletions (fill-in-the-blank) for facts and image occlusion for diagrams. This applies to any spaced-repetition app (Anki, SuperMemo, RemNote, Mochi and others), not only to Anki.

parts.why: A spaced-repetition app is a scheduler for active recall: it shows you each card just before you would forget it, and pushes cards you know well further into the future. That puts your time where forgetting is about to happen, which is why a few minutes a day can hold thousands of facts. The catch is that the app only schedules; the quality of what you remember depends on how the card is written. A vague card is like a key cut slightly wrong: it sometimes opens the lock, and you never know why.
parts.how:
1. Make cards the same day, while the material still makes sense to you.
  2. Write each card so it has one clear, short answer. If a card asks for a list of seven things, split it or turn it into overlapping clozes.
  3. Do your due reviews first every day. New cards only after reviews are done; a backlog of reviews is how most people quit.
  4. Use cloze deletions for facts in context, image occlusion for diagrams and maps, and reversed cards only where you need both directions (word to meaning, meaning to word).
  5. Add a little context to the front ("Contract law:", "Python lists:") so similar cards do not get confused.
  6. Delete or rewrite any card you keep failing. Repeated failure usually means a bad card, not a bad memory.

Two short guides are worth reading once before you write many cards: Piotr Wozniak's "20 rules of formulating knowledge" (understand before you memorise, keep items minimal, avoid sets and enumerations) and Andy Matuschak's prompt-writing guide (good prompts are focused, precise, consistent, and require real retrieval rather than guessing).

examples.simple: A French learner turns "la voiture (f.), the car" into a cloze card: "{{c1::La}} voiture est rouge." The card tests the gender in a real sentence, which is what she actually gets wrong when speaking.
examples.nontrivial: A law student first writes "What are the elements of negligence?" and keeps failing it, because it asks for four things at once. She rewrites it as four cards ("Negligence: after duty of care, the claimant must show a {{c1::breach}} of that duty", and so on) plus one card that asks "Which element fails when the harm was not reasonably foreseeable?" The small cards hold the facts; the last card makes her use them.
examples.html:
• Simple: A French learner turns "la voiture (f.), the car" into a cloze card: "{{c1::La}} voiture est rouge." The card tests the gender in a real sentence, which is what she actually gets wrong when speaking.
  • Non-trivial: A law student first writes "What are the elements of negligence?" and keeps failing it, because it asks for four things at once. She rewrites it as four cards ("Negligence: after duty of care, the claimant must show a {{c1::breach}} of that duty", and so on) plus one card that asks "Which element fails when the harm was not reasonably foreseeable?" The small cards hold the facts; the last card makes her use them.

parts.time: Making 2-4 cards for a paragraph takes ~3-5 min (~6-10×); each later review takes ~10-20 s (~0.5×). The card-making is the expensive part, so only card what you will really need. These are rough estimates, not measurements.
parts.watch:
• Adding new cards every day until reviews take two hours. Set a daily cap for new cards (for example 10-20) and keep it.
  • Cards that can be answered by recognising the shape of the question instead of recalling the answer.
  • Copying whole sentences from the book. If a card is longer than two lines, it is probably two cards.

items.title: Premade decks
items.leadHtml: Shared decks save hours, but only if they match your course content. Turn on (unsuspend) just the cards that match what you are currently studying instead of the whole deck. Examples include the AnKing deck for US medical licensing exams, frequency-ordered vocabulary decks for languages, decks built to follow a particular textbook, and community decks for things like country capitals, the periodic table or kanji.

parts.why: Making cards is the most expensive step of spaced repetition, so a good deck written by someone else hands you hundreds of hours of work for free. But you pay in a different coin. When you write a card yourself you have already thought about the fact once (the generation effect), and the card fits the way your course frames it. A premade card arrives cold: it may be correct and still feel like a stranger's sentence. The best use is a hybrid: borrow the wording, but only for what you have just learned.
parts.how:
1. Check fit first: compare 20 random cards with your syllabus or textbook. If many are irrelevant or framed differently, the deck will cost more than it saves.
  2. Suspend everything, then unsuspend by tag or chapter as you cover each topic in class.
  3. Edit freely. Add your lecturer's example, your own mnemonic or a picture to cards that will not stick.
  4. Write your own cards for anything the deck misses, especially what your lecturer stressed.

examples.simple: A Japanese learner uses a shared kanji deck but unlocks only the 15 kanji from this week's textbook chapter, so reviews and lessons reinforce each other.
examples.nontrivial: A medical student on the AnKing deck notices her own course teaches a topic differently from the US exam the deck was built for. She keeps the deck's cards for shared basics, suspends the ones on content her exams do not test, and adds 10 own cards with her lecturer's framing. The deck becomes a base, not a syllabus.

  • Non-trivial: A medical student on the AnKing deck notices her own course teaches a topic differently from the US exam the deck was built for. She keeps the deck's cards for shared basics, suspends the ones on content her exams do not test, and adds 10 own cards with her lecturer's framing. The deck becomes a base, not a syllabus.

parts.time: You skip most of the card-making cost (~3-5 min, ~6-10× per paragraph) and pay only for reviews (~10-20 s, ~0.5× per card) plus a few minutes per week to unsuspend and edit. Rough estimates.
parts.watch:
• Turning on the whole deck at once. Thousands of new cards on topics you have not met are just noise, and the review pile becomes unmanageable.
  • Learning a deck instead of a course. If your exam is written by your lecturer, the deck is a helper, not the spine.

items.title: Don't let cards replace understanding
items.leadHtml: Learn the mechanism or the reasoning first, then card the details. A card you can't explain is a card you will forget.

parts.why: A fact you understand is held in place by many threads: what causes it, what it causes, what it is similar to. A fact learned alone hangs on one thread, the card itself, and that thread snaps under exam pressure or when the question is worded differently. Understanding also tells you which details matter. People given a confusing passage remember far less of it than people who first see what it is about, even though the words are identical.
parts.how:
1. Study the topic first: explain it to yourself, draw it, or do a few problems.
  2. Only then make cards, and make them for the details that hang on the structure you now see.
  3. Add at least one "why" or "what follows" card per topic, not only "what" cards.
  4. When a card keeps failing, go back to the source and ask what you did not understand, before rewriting the card.

examples.simple: In chemistry, "Group 1 metals react violently with water" is easy to card. Knowing they have one outer electron they give up easily makes the card almost unnecessary, and also tells you why reactivity increases down the group.
examples.nontrivial: A programming student has cards for 30 Git commands and still panics at merge conflicts. After spending an hour on how Git stores commits as a graph, half the commands become obvious consequences, and her remaining cards ("What does rebase do to the commit graph?") are fewer and better.

items.title: Mnemonics and acronyms
items.leadHtml: Useful for arbitrary lists like the cranial nerves, the order of the planets, the causes of a condition or the notes on a stave. Make them silly, vivid and personal. Commercial versions such as Sketchy and Pixorize use picture stories for subjects like microbiology and pharmacology.

parts.why: A mnemonic does not make the facts meaningful; it borrows meaning from something you already know well and hangs the facts on it. Your memory is good at vivid, odd, emotional images and at sentences, and poor at strings of unrelated items. A mnemonic translates the second into the first. It works like a luggage tag: the bag (the knowledge) is still yours to pack, but the tag makes it findable.
parts.how:
1. Use mnemonics only for material without its own logic: lists, orders, word-to-meaning pairs.
  2. Pick the type: an acronym (the first letters spell a word), an acrostic (a sentence whose words start with the letters), or a keyword image (a sound-alike word linked to the meaning).
  3. Make it vivid, absurd or personal. "My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos" is remembered because it is a little odd.
  4. Test the mnemonic, then the facts behind it. Make a card for both.

examples.simple: Music students learn the treble-clef lines E, G, B, D, F with "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit."
examples.nontrivial: A Spanish learner uses the keyword method for "pato" (duck): she imagines a duck being patted on the head. It works for a few hundred hard words, but she notices the image fades once she has used the word in conversation a few times. That is the ideal outcome: the mnemonic was scaffolding, and the real memory has replaced it.

  • Non-trivial: A Spanish learner uses the keyword method for "pato" (duck): she imagines a duck being patted on the head. It works for a few hundred hard words, but she notices the image fades once she has used the word in conversation a few times. That is the ideal outcome: the mnemonic was scaffolding, and the real memory has replaced it.

parts.time: ~2-5 min to build a mnemonic for one list (~4-10×). Cheap for a list you need for years, expensive if you make one for every fact. Rough estimates.
parts.watch:
• A mnemonic for something you could understand instead. It gives you the words without the meaning.
  • Too many similar mnemonics. Ten acrostics about ten lists start to blur into each other.

items.title: Memory palace (method of loci)
items.leadHtml: Place items along a route through a familiar place, such as your home. It works well for ordered lists.

parts.why: Human memory for places is very strong: you can walk through your home in your mind and never miss a room. The memory palace uses that existing map as a set of hooks. Each item becomes a vivid image left at a fixed spot, and walking the route gives you the items back in order. Memory champions use this almost without exception, and ordinary people who trained it for six weeks more than doubled their recall of word lists.
parts.how:
1. Choose a place you know very well and a fixed route through it (front door, hall, kitchen, sofa, window...).
  2. Turn each item into a concrete, exaggerated image.
  3. Place one image at each spot and make it interact with the spot (it is melting on the sofa, singing in the sink).
  4. Walk the route in your mind a few times, then recall without looking.
  5. Review it like any other material, spaced over days.

examples.simple: To remember a shopping list, you picture a giant egg blocking the front door, milk flooding the hall and bread used as a pillow on the sofa.
examples.nontrivial: A history student needs the order of the English monarchs for an essay exam. She puts each one along her daily walk to campus, with an image for the key event of the reign at each landmark. Because the route has an order, she can also answer "who came after Henry VII?" by stepping forward one place, and the event images give her dates and context for free.

• Simple: To remember a shopping list, you picture a giant egg blocking the front door, milk flooding the hall and bread used as a pillow on the sofa.
  • Non-trivial: A history student needs the order of the English monarchs for an essay exam. She puts each one along her daily walk to campus, with an image for the key event of the reign at each landmark. Because the route has an order, she can also answer "who came after Henry VII?" by stepping forward one place, and the event images give her dates and context for free.

parts.watch:
• Using it for material that needs understanding. A palace stores order and names, not reasons.
  • Reusing the same palace for many lists too soon. Old images interfere with new ones; use several routes.

items.title: Chunking
items.leadHtml: Group items into meaningful clusters (for example, drugs by mechanism, verbs by conjugation pattern, cases by legal principle) instead of memorising them one by one.

parts.why: Working memory can only juggle a handful of items at once, but an "item" can be large if it is meaningful. A chess master does not see 25 pieces; she sees four or five familiar patterns. A phone number is easier as 0207 946 0123 than as ten digits. Chunking turns many small things into a few big ones, and the grouping itself carries information: once you know the group, each member is half remembered already.
parts.how:
1. Lay out the whole list in front of you.
  2. Look for a meaningful rule that sorts it: same mechanism, same ending, same period, same cause.
  3. Name each group and learn the rule first, then the members.
  4. Learn the exceptions separately and on purpose; they are where exam questions live.

examples.simple: Instead of 20 German prepositions one by one, you learn them as four groups by the case they take (accusative, dative, two-way, genitive). One rule now covers five words at a time.
examples.nontrivial: An economics student memorises 30 historical financial crises one by one and keeps confusing them. She regroups them by cause (bank runs, currency pegs breaking, asset bubbles, sovereign debt). The groups make her see a pattern she can use in an essay, and the odd ones that fit no group turn out to be the most interesting ones.
examples.html:
• Simple: Instead of 20 German prepositions one by one, you learn them as four groups by the case they take (accusative, dative, two-way, genitive). One rule now covers five words at a time.
  • Non-trivial: An economics student memorises 30 historical financial crises one by one and keeps confusing them. She regroups them by cause (bank runs, currency pegs breaking, asset bubbles, sovereign debt). The groups make her see a pattern she can use in an essay, and the odd ones that fit no group turn out to be the most interesting ones.

parts.time: ~2-5 min to group a list (~4-10×). Often the best value of all memory tricks, because it also builds understanding. Rough estimates.
parts.watch: Groups that are arbitrary (alphabetical, by lecture number) do not help much. The grouping should be one you would want to know anyway.

She regroups them by cause (bank runs, currency pegs breaking, asset bubbles, sovereign debt). The groups make her see a pattern she can use in an essay, and the odd ones that fit no group turn out to be the most interesting ones.

⏱ Time cost. ~2-5 min to group a list (~4-10×). Often the best value of all memory tricks, because it also builds understanding. Rough estimates.

Watch out. Groups that are arbitrary (alphabetical, by lecture number) do not help much. The grouping should be one you would want to know anyway.

items.title: Spaced reviews for whole topics too
items.leadHtml: Not everything needs a flashcard. Reviewing a whole topic by blank-page recall on day 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 covers understanding as well as facts.

parts.why: Flashcards test pieces; exams and real use ask you to put pieces together. Writing out a whole topic from memory tests the structure: what comes first, what causes what, where each detail belongs. Spacing those attempts gives the same benefit as spaced flashcards, applied to the whole map instead of single facts. Think of cards as checking the bricks and whole-topic recall as checking the building.
parts.how:
1. After first learning a topic, schedule reviews at growing gaps (for example 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days).
  2. At each review, take a blank page and write or sketch everything you remember about the topic for 10-15 minutes.
  3. Check against your notes and fill the gaps in another colour.
  4. If a review went well, stretch the next gap; if it went badly, shorten it.
  5. Turn the facts you keep missing into flashcards.

examples.simple: A physics student reviews "circular motion" by writing the key equations and drawing the force diagrams from memory on day 1, 3 and 7.
examples.nontrivial: A history student studying the French Revolution finds she can answer all her date cards but cannot write a coherent paragraph on why the monarchy fell. Whole-topic recall on day 7 shows the problem: she knows the events but not the causal chain. She adds a timeline with arrows to her review and lets the date cards run on their own.
examples.html:
• Simple: A physics student reviews "circular motion" by writing the key equations and drawing the force diagrams from memory on day 1, 3 and 7.
  • Non-trivial: A history student studying the French Revolution finds she can answer all her date cards but cannot write a coherent paragraph on why the monarchy fell. Whole-topic recall on day 7 shows the problem: she knows the events but not the causal chain. She adds a timeline with arrows to her review and lets the date cards run on their own.

parts.time: Each review is a blank-page recall: ~2 min per paragraph's worth (~4×). Five reviews over a month come to ~10 min per paragraph in total, spread out, though in practice a one-page dump covers a whole topic in outline and is cheaper per paragraph. Rough estimates.
parts.watch:
• Reviewing by re-reading notes instead of writing from memory. That is the low-value version.
  • Losing track of what is due. Keep a simple list or calendar of topics and review dates.
